title: He befriended a backyard deer. She taught him life lessons.
text:
He befriended a backyard deer. She taught him life lessons.
In “Penelope: A Love Story,” Paul Bochner chronicles what he calls “one of the greatest loves I have ever known,” a relationship that brings him “an inexpressible joy.” He and Penelope “are soulmates,” he writes.
It’s not what you think: Penelope is the name Bochner gives a white-tailed deer that was born in a wooded area beside his house in New York’s Hudson Valley. Bochner first encounters the newborn fawn in June 2014. When he next observes her a few weeks later, her leg is badly injured and she has been abandoned by her mother.
Bochner assumes that the mother has rejected her unhealthy offspring to avoid slowing down the herd and drawing predators. He further assumes that the fawn will not survive the winter. In March 2015, however, the deer, frail and emaciated, reappears outside of his home. Bochner places apple pieces on the ground between them and speaks soothingly to her. From that point on, she returns every day.
Paul Bochner’s debut book details his unexpected connection with a fawn and how his selfless care for the animal blessed him, too.
“Penelope” is the first book by Bochner, a filmmaker who has written for The New Yorker and The Atlantic. His tender and surprising memoir charts the progression of his relationship with the deer that he calls Penelope. He attributes his immediate affinity for the forsaken animal to his “own abandonment anxiety,” the result, he explains, of feeling neglected when he was a child.
As Penelope’s trust in him grows, she allows their contact to advance by increments. Over time, she takes her food from his hand; allows him to stroke her fur; holds his hand in her mouth for several minutes before feedings; grooms him by licking his hands and arms; and presses her face against his. Eventually she is comfortable enough to enter his house.
Just as remarkable as a wild deer’s attachment to a human is this particular human’s devotion to a wild deer. Bochner, single and in his 60s when Penelope enters his life (he has since married), organizes his schedule around her twice-daily feedings. He wakes at dawn to be outside when she arrives, declines social invitations that will prevent him from being home in the evening, and avoids travel unless absolutely necessary. Penelope roams freely when she’s not with the author, and he frets over the dangers posed by coyotes, foxes, and cars. One believes him when he claims, “I do place Penelope’s well-being above my own.”
On the rare occasions when Bochner must leave town, he recruits neighbors to put out food in his absence. Even so, Penelope expresses what he perceives to be anger upon his return, either failing to show up at his house or, in one case, after he is away for several days, aggressively biting his hand. “She punishes me for my lapses,” he notes.
These reactions persuade the author that Penelope has an inner life – that she experiences a range of emotions and understands cause and effect.
Bochner’s prose is elegant and direct. In addition to being almost unbearably moving, the memoir has moments of humor. One day a young male deer follows Penelope into Bochner’s yard and warily observes that morning’s feeding. Afterward, Penelope leads the author over to the buck. “It felt as if she were introducing me to her date,” he recalls.
Bochner is thrilled when Penelope later gives birth. While many homeowners regard the animals as pests, Bochner encourages deer to make use of his property, well aware that they occupied the land long before humans did. The author admires the gentle herbivores that “take only what they need to survive.”
While he is welcoming to all deer, his kinship with one singular deer ends up affirming his most deeply held views.
“Since childhood I had felt that, in life generally, those things which connect and unite us are greater and more substantial than those which separate and divide,” he writes. “My broad and reflexive belief that the lines of demarcation can be dissolved, and indeed that every form of goodness might flow from this dissolution, was now being demonstrated in the physical world.”
We hear much about separation and division these days. Bochner’s hopeful account conveys an implicit message: If a meaningful connection can exist between a person and a wild animal, perhaps unlikely connections can be forged between people across seemingly uncrossable boundaries, too.
